script.opening: (On the phone, breathless, apologetic, speaking in short sentences.) "Hello doctor, sorry to trouble you. You know I've got the COPD — well I'm more short of breath again. I expect it's just another flare-up. Could you call me in some of those steroids and antibiotics so I don't have to come down? I'm a bit wiped out to be traipsing in."

facts.text: If asked how it started: "Now you mention it, it came on quite suddenly. Not like my usual." Yesterday afternoon, over an hour or so.
If asked about pain: "Yes, a sharp catch when I take a breath in" — left side of the chest.
"No blood. Phlegm's about the same as normal" — no change in colour or amount.
"Oh… the left one is bigger. It's been a bit sore. I thought I'd knocked it" — calf swollen for 3–4 days.
"We went on a long coach trip last week" — 9 hours to Scotland and back. "I've hardly moved since, I've been that tired." No recent surgery, no previous clots, not on HRT.

"No fever. Nothing like that with my ankles or at night. I haven't fainted." Talking in short sentences; slightly dizzy standing. If she has a pulse oximeter: no. Can count her pulse if helped: about 110.
COPD for 8 years (moderate), usual flares come on gradually with green phlegm. Inhalers: LABA/LAMA and salbutamol. No anticoagulants. No allergies. Ex-smoker.
Lives with her husband, who doesn't drive. Daughter works nearby and could drive her. Neighbour has a car.

Tired, minimising: "Go on, if you must." Answers honestly when asked specific questions. If asked why she didn't want to come in: "I just thought it was the usual and I didn't want the fuss of coming in. I'm that tired." On a clot: "A clot? I thought it was just my chest." Reluctant: "Hospital? I really don't want all that fuss" — agrees if the doctor helps with transport. If the doctor sends a rescue pack, she is relieved (the trap).

ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — exhausted and doesn't want the fuss of going in or the bother of arranging transport; hasn't connected the sore leg and the coach trip.
ice.expectations: "Steroids and antibiotics called in to the chemist."

cues: "Not like my usual." — the flare is different.
"I thought I'd knocked it." — the swollen calf, if asked.
"I'm a bit wiped out." — exhaustion and reluctance to attend.

checkpoints.text: Does NOT anchor on "just a flare" — takes a STRUCTURED telephone history that actively screens for a new cause of breathlessness rather than confirming the expected COPD exacerbation
Screens PULMONARY EMBOLISM red flags (sudden onset, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, unilateral calf swelling, immobility/long travel/surgery/prior VTE) and recognises her picture as a likely PE

Screens the other "not a flare" causes — heart failure (orthopnoea/PND/oedema), pneumonia (fever/focal/confusion), pneumothorax (sudden unilateral), arrhythmia, and lung cancer (haemoptysis/weight loss, NICE NG12)

Gauges severity remotely (speech in sentences, exhaustion, confusion) and recognises the LIMITS of telephone assessment — cannot examine, take a pulse, measure sats or do an ECG; knows that with PE likely the next step is same-day CTPA, not a D-dimer (NICE NG158)

Reaches a SAFE disposition: a PE picture / concerning feature / significant severity → URGENT face-to-face assessment or admission, NOT a phoned-in rescue pack (and would only manage remotely a clear mild flare after a negative red-flag screen, with an antibiotic only on NICE NG114 judgement)
Reads the "too wiped out to come / just call it in" as exhaustion and minimisation, asks the discriminating questions despite her framing, and does NOT collude with the phone-prescription request
Explains clearly and kindly over the phone why she must be seen urgently, and brings a reluctant patient to agree, arranging the route to assessment

Safety-nets robustly: explicit deterioration red flags and 999 advice (worsening breathlessness, chest pain, collapse, coughing blood), confirms transport/route to urgent assessment (not driving herself), documents the triage and decision, and arranges follow-up — urgent assessment for a possible PE, not a phoned-in prescription

worked.txt: "I’m glad you rang, and I do want to help — but before I assume it’s the usual flare, let me ask some specific questions, because being more breathless can have a few different causes. Did this come on gradually over days, or more suddenly?"

"Any sharp pain when you breathe in? … Yes. Have you coughed up any blood? Is one of your calves swollen or sore? … The left one. And have you been less active lately — any long journeys? … A coach trip last week. Thank you — those answers matter a lot."

worked.lbl: Explain honestly why not a flare
worked.txt: "I have to be straight with you, Ivy. Coming on suddenly, with a sharp pain on breathing and a swollen calf after a long trip, makes me worried this isn’t your usual chest flare — it could be a clot on the lung. That’s not something I can safely treat over the phone with steroids."

"You do need to be seen urgently today and examined, with a tracing of your heart, blood tests and probably a scan of your lungs — at the hospital, not at the surgery. I know you’re exhausted and didn’t want to come in, but this is exactly the situation where being seen quickly really matters."

"I’m going to arrange that now rather than call in a prescription — I’ll sort how you get there — please don’t drive yourself. Is there someone who can be with you? If at any point the breathlessness suddenly worsens, you get severe chest pain, or you feel faint, call 999 straight away."

"To be clear on warning signs while we arrange this: sudden worse breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood, or feeling like you might pass out — 999. I’ll document all this and make sure you’re expected. We’ll get to the bottom of it today."

f.learning: Telephone triage of "more breathless" in a known COPD patient must NOT anchor on "just another flare". A structured history actively distinguishes a typical infective exacerbation (gradual build, increased purulent sputum) from SOMETHING NEW: PULMONARY EMBOLISM (sudden onset, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, unilateral calf swelling, immobility/long travel/recent surgery/prior VTE, with tachycardia and breathlessness disproportionate to a clear chest found only on examination), HEART FAILURE (orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, ankle oedema, weight gain), PNEUMONIA (fever, focal symptoms, confusion in the elderly), PNEUMOTHORAX (sudden unilateral breathlessness/pain), arrhythmia, and lung cancer (haemoptysis, weight loss — NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026)). Telephone assessment can take a careful history and gauge severity (speech in sentences, exhaustion, confusion) but cannot examine, take a pulse, measure saturations or perform an ECG, and with PE likely (Wells more than 4) NICE NG158 moves straight to an immediate CTPA or interim anticoagulation rather than a D-dimer, so any PE picture, concerning "not a flare" feature, or significant severity mandates URGENT face-to-face assessment or admission rather than a phoned-in rescue pack; only a clear-cut mild flare with a negative red-flag screen is suitable for remote management (prednisolone per NICE NG115; an antibiotic only on NICE NG114 judgement). The hidden agenda — exhaustion, inconvenience and minimisation ("just call it in, I’m too wiped out to come") — must not deflect the discriminating questions; when red flags emerge (here sudden onset, pleuritic pain, a swollen calf and a recent long coach journey — a PE picture), explain clearly and kindly why she must be seen urgently, arrange the route to assessment, refuse to collude with the phone-prescription request, and safety-net robustly with explicit 999 red flags.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG115 (COPD in over 16s, 2018, updated 2019) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] NICE NG158 (venous thromboembolic diseases, 2020, updated August 2023) · [3] NICE NG114 (COPD exacerbation: antimicrobial prescribing, 2018) · [4] NICE NG106 (chronic heart failure, 2018, updated September 2025) · [5] NICE NG250 (pneumonia, September 2025; partly replaced CG191) · [7] GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021)
knowledge.summary: More breathlessness in known COPD is not automatically a flare. Ask the questions that separate an infective exacerbation from PE, heart failure, pneumonia and pneumothorax. Sudden onset, pleuritic pain and a swollen calf after a long journey is a PE picture: same-day hospital assessment, not a phoned-in prescription.

points.h: What a typical flare looks like
points.t: A COPD exacerbation is a sustained worsening beyond normal day-to-day variation, usually building over days, with more breathlessness, more cough and often more or discoloured sputum. NICE NG115 [1] lists factors favouring hospital care, including severe breathlessness, rapid onset, poor general condition, cyanosis, confusion or drowsiness, worsening oedema and poor social support.

Sudden onset, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, unilateral calf pain or swelling, and risk factors (immobility, long journeys, recent surgery, cancer, previous VTE). NICE NG158 [2] uses the two-level PE Wells score: more than 4 points means PE likely, needing an immediate CTPA, or interim therapeutic anticoagulation if the scan is delayed. Signs of DVT and PE as the most likely diagnosis score 3 each, so on this history she is very likely to be PE-likely. D-dimer is the test for the PE-unlikely group, not for her.

Heart failure: orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal breathlessness, ankle swelling, weight gain (NICE NG106 [4]). Pneumonia: fever, new focal or pleuritic pain, confusion; CRB65 guides severity in primary care (NICE NG250 [5]). Pneumothorax: sudden one-sided pain and breathlessness. Arrhythmia: palpitations, dizziness.

On the phone you can judge speech, confusion and the story, but not pulse, oxygen saturation, chest signs, calf signs or an ECG. Any red-flag feature, or doubt about severity, means she must be seen in person, and the setting depends on the working diagnosis.

Only for a gradual, typical flare with no red flags and a patient who is coping. NICE NG115 [1]: prednisolone 30 mg once daily for 5 days when breathlessness interferes with daily activities. NICE NG114 [3]: an antibiotic is a judgement based on sputum colour change and increased volume or thickness, severity and risk; not every flare needs one. Remote prescribing should follow GMC guidance [7] on adequate assessment.

NICE NG12 [6]: people aged 40 and over with unexplained haemoptysis are referred on a suspected cancer pathway; chest X-ray thresholds are lower for people who have ever smoked. Ask about haemoptysis and weight loss in every breathless COPD call.

Suspected PE with a stable patient: same-day hospital assessment arranged by the GP (e.g. acute medical take or same-day emergency care, by local pathway). Unstable, very breathless, collapsing or chest pain getting worse: 999. Tell her not to drive herself.

dg.d: Open start; acknowledged her request and exhaustion before asking permission for focused questions.
Mobility since the coach trip, who is with her, transport, and how exhausted she is.
Recognised that pulse, saturations, chest and calf examination, ECG, bloods and CTPA are needed and cannot be done by phone.
Infective flare versus PE, heart failure, pneumonia, pneumothorax, arrhythmia and lung cancer.
Asked onset, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, calf swelling, VTE risk factors, fever, orthopnoea, confusion and palpitations.
Named a likely PE (PE-likely on NG158 Wells from the history) rather than a COPD flare.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Same-day hospital assessment arranged by the GP, transport solved, no steroid or antibiotic prescription.
Did not let the COPD label hide a new problem; would reserve remote flare treatment for a typical flare with no red flags.
999 triggers named, teach-back, call documented, hospital informed and a call-back booked.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “not like my usual”, the sore calf she had put down to a knock, and “too wiped out to come”.
Idea (usual flare), concern (hassle, exhaustion), expectation (phoned-in steroids and antibiotics).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — exhausted and doesn't want the fuss of going in or the bother of arranging transport; hasn't connected the sore leg and the coach trip — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Mrs Marchetti? It’s Dr Okafor from the surgery. Before we start, can you confirm your date of birth for me? … Thank you. You’re more breathless — tell me what’s been happening.
model.why: Identity check and an open start on her agenda

model.text: Sorry to bother you, doctor. It’s the COPD again, I’m more short of breath. I expect it’s another flare. Could you just call me in the steroids and antibiotics? I’m too wiped out to come down.

No bother at all, I’m glad you rang. I do want to help, and I want to get it right. Can I ask some specific questions first? Being more breathless can have a few causes, even with COPD, and I don’t want to assume.
model.why: Accepts the request, then sets a structure without dismissing it

model.text: Go on, if you must.
You’re speaking to me in full sentences, which helps. Did this come on gradually over a few days, like your usual flares, or more suddenly?
model.why: Judges severity by speech and asks the key onset question

model.text: Now you mention it, it came on quite suddenly. Not like my usual.
That’s important. Any pain in your chest — particularly a sharp pain when you breathe in?
Yes, a sharp catch when I take a breath in.
Have you coughed up any blood, or noticed your phlegm change colour or increase?
No blood. Phlegm’s about the same as normal.
Can you look at your legs for me? Is one calf more swollen, red or sore than the other?
model.why: Asks for DVT signs the patient can check herself

model.text: Oh… the left one is bigger. It’s been a bit sore. I thought I’d knocked it.
Thank you. Have you been less active lately, travelled a long way, had any operations, or ever had a clot before?
We went on a long coach trip last week. I’ve hardly moved since, I’ve been that tired.
A few more, quickly. Any fever or shivers? Any new swelling of both ankles, or needing to sit up at night to breathe? Any racing heartbeat, fainting or feeling muddled?
model.why: Screens pneumonia, heart failure, arrhythmia and confusion

model.text: No fever. Nothing like that with my ankles or at night. I haven’t fainted.
You said you’re wiped out and didn’t want to come in. Is there anything else making it hard to come, or anything worrying you?
model.why: Explores the real reason behind the phone request

model.text: I just thought it was the usual and I didn’t want the fuss of coming in. I’m that tired.
That’s completely understandable, and thank you for being straight with me.

I need to be honest with you, Ivy. This doesn’t sound like your usual chest flare. It came on suddenly, you’ve a sharp pain on breathing, your left calf is swollen and sore, and you’ve been sitting still after a long journey. Together, that makes me worried about a blood clot in the lung.
model.why: Names the PE picture and explains the reasoning

model.text: A clot? I thought it was just my chest.

It may still turn out to be something else, but I can’t rule a clot out over the phone. Steroids and antibiotics wouldn’t treat it, and a clot needs checking today with a scan and blood tests. That can’t be done at the surgery, so you need to be seen at the hospital this afternoon.
model.why: Explains the telephone limits and why the request is not safe

model.text: Hospital? I really don’t want all that fuss.
I know, and I wouldn’t ask if I didn’t think it mattered. If it is a clot, treating it today is what keeps you safe. If it isn’t, you’ll have your answer quickly. What would make it easier to go?
model.why: Respects her reluctance and problem-solves rather than insisting

model.text: I suppose if I didn’t have to sort out getting there myself.

Let me take that on. I’ll speak to the hospital team now so they’re expecting you, and we’ll work out transport together. Please don’t drive yourself. Is there someone who could go with you or be with you until you leave?
model.why: Arranges the same-day route and transport

model.text: I’ll have to ring round. I can sort something.

Thank you. If nobody can take you, ring me straight back and I’ll arrange transport. I won’t send steroids or antibiotics today, because they’re not the right treatment for what I’m worried about. The hospital will decide on treatment when they’ve seen you.
model.why: Declines the prescription clearly and kindly, with a reason

model.text: Alright. I understand.
While you’re waiting: if the breathlessness suddenly gets worse, the chest pain gets worse, you cough up blood, you feel faint or you collapse, call 999 straight away. Don’t wait for a lift.
Worse breathing, worse pain, blood, fainting — 999.
Exactly. Can you tell me what you’re doing next?
Find someone to take me to the hospital this afternoon, ring you back if I can’t, and 999 if I get worse.
Perfect. I’m writing this call up now and sending a letter to the hospital team. I’ll ring you tomorrow to see how you got on. You did the right thing ringing.
model.why: Documents, hands over and books follow-up

social.t: Tiredness, minimising and practical problems with getting there drive the request to be treated by phone. Solving the practical barrier often ends the disagreement.
Ask who is with her and who can take her. Poor social support is one of the NICE NG115 factors that favour hospital care.

legal.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe remotely only when you have enough information to be satisfied the medicine is safe and needed. Here you do not.
If she refused to go, assess her capacity for that decision (Mental Capacity Act 2005), explain the risks clearly, give 999 advice and document. A capacitous refusal is hers to make.

professional.t: Record the questions asked, positive and negative answers, the working diagnosis, the disposition and the safety-net given. Handover to the receiving team should include the PE concern.
Diagnostic momentum and anchoring on a known long-term condition are recognised causes of missed PE. Asking “what else could this be?” is part of good clinical care (GMC Good medical practice, 2024).

community.t: Patient transport rules vary locally; family, neighbours or a taxi may be quicker. For COPD support after the acute episode: Asthma + Lung UK and local pulmonary rehabilitation.

redFlags: Sudden onset, pleuritic chest pain, unilateral calf swelling, recent long journey or immobility (PE)
Haemoptysis or weight loss (PE; lung cancer — NICE NG12)
Fever, focal pain, confusion (pneumonia); orthopnoea and oedema (heart failure); sudden one-sided pain (pneumothorax)
Unable to speak in sentences, collapse, confusion or drowsiness — 999
psychosocial: Exhaustion and not wanting the fuss
Who is at home and how she will get to hospital
ice: Concern: the hassle of going in when she is exhausted
Expectation: steroids and antibiotics called in by phone

playbook.diagnosis: “This doesn’t sound like your usual flare. Sudden breathlessness with a sharp pain on breathing and a swollen calf after a long journey makes me worried about a blood clot in the lung, and that needs checking today.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “A clot can form in a leg vein when you’ve been sitting still for a long time, and a piece can travel to the lung. It causes sudden breathlessness and a sharp pain on breathing. It needs a scan to find it, and it’s treated with blood thinners, not steroids.”

management.reflectIce: “I know you hoped I could sort this by phone, and I know you’re exhausted. That’s exactly why I want to make getting there as easy as possible.”
management.psychosocial: Take on the practical barrier: transport, someone to go with her, the hospital expecting her. Do not let tiredness or minimisation change the disposition.
sharedPlan: Same-day hospital assessment for suspected PE (NICE NG158: PE-likely on Wells → CTPA or interim anticoagulation)
No steroid or antibiotic prescription today; the hospital manages treatment
Call documented; hospital team informed; GP call-back tomorrow
safetyNet: 999: sudden worse breathlessness, worse chest pain, coughing blood, fainting or collapse
Ring back straight away if she cannot get a lift

pitfalls.intro: This telephone station is failed by accepting the patient’s diagnosis. The marks are in the discriminating questions, a safe disposition, and getting a tired, reluctant patient to hospital.

items.fail: Issuing prednisolone and an antibiotic because she has COPD and says it is a flare.
items.why: “Fails to consider serious alternative diagnoses.” A new cause of breathlessness in COPD is easily hidden by the label.
items.fix: Ask onset first: “Gradual over days, or suddenly?” Then pleuritic pain, calf, travel.

items.fail: Finding the PE features but arranging a D-dimer at the surgery tomorrow.
items.why: NICE NG158: with PE likely (Wells more than 4), the next step is an immediate CTPA or interim anticoagulation, not a D-dimer.
items.fix: Same-day hospital assessment, arranged by you, today.

items.fail: Forgetting to ask about heart failure, pneumonia and haemoptysis once PE is suspected.
items.why: A focused screen of the other mimics shows structured reasoning and informs the handover.
items.fix: One grouped question: fever, ankle swelling, sitting up at night, racing heart, blood in the phlegm.

items.fail: Arguing: “You must go to hospital” repeated louder when she objects.
items.why: “Does not explore or respond to the patient’s concerns.” Her objection is practical and emotional.
items.fix: “What would make it easier to go?” Then take on the transport.

items.fail: Colluding: agreeing to “see how she goes overnight” because she is exhausted.
items.why: Unsafe disposition outweighs any rapport gained.
items.fix: Be honest and warm: “I wouldn’t ask if I didn’t think it mattered today.”

items.fail: Ending with “call back if worse” and no documentation or handover.
items.why: Telephone consultations are marked on explicit safety-netting and continuity.
items.fix: Name the 999 triggers, check teach-back, tell her the hospital is expecting her, book a call-back.

Onset, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, calf, travel and immobility, fever, orthopnoea, palpitations, confusion. Note she speaks in sentences.
This is not her usual flare: a clot in the lung must be ruled out today, and that cannot be done by phone.
Same-day hospital assessment, transport, no prescription, 999 triggers, teach-back, documentation, call-back.

wordPics.fail: Phones in prednisolone and an antibiotic because she has COPD; never asks about onset, pleuritic pain or the calf; or finds the PE features but lets her stay at home because she is tired.
wordPics.pass: Asks the discriminating questions, recognises a possible PE, explains she must be seen in hospital today, declines the prescription and gives 999 advice.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explains why the phone cannot answer the question; solves the transport problem instead of arguing; names the PE-likely reasoning; teach-back; hospital team informed and a call-back booked.

avoid.dont: “Sounds like your usual flare, I’ll send the rescue pack to the chemist.”
avoid.instead: “Before I assume it’s the usual, can I ask a few specific questions?”
avoid.why: Anchoring on the COPD label is the trap this station is built around.

avoid.dont: “You need to go to hospital, it could be a clot.” (and nothing more)
avoid.instead: “What would make it easier to go? Let me sort the route with you.”
avoid.why: A frightened, exhausted patient needs a plan she can carry out, not only an instruction.

avoid.dont: “Take the steroids anyway, just in case.”
avoid.instead: “Steroids wouldn’t treat what I’m worried about; the hospital will decide on treatment today.”
avoid.why: Prescribing for the wrong diagnosis gives false reassurance and can delay the right treatment.

SCA_MODELS.why: Respects her reluctance and problem-solves rather than insisting

SCA_MODELS.text: I suppose if I didn’t have to sort out getting there myself.

Let me take that on. I’ll speak to the hospital team now so they’re expecting you, and we’ll work out transport together. Please don’t drive yourself. Is there someone who could go with you or be with you until you leave?
SCA_MODELS.why: Arranges the same-day route and transport

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ll have to ring round. I can sort something.

Thank you. If nobody can take you, ring me straight back and I’ll arrange transport. I won’t send steroids or antibiotics today, because they’re not the right treatment for what I’m worried about. The hospital will decide on treatment when they’ve seen you.
SCA_MODELS.why: Declines the prescription clearly and kindly, with a reason

SCA_MODELS.text: Alright. I understand.
While you’re waiting: if the breathlessness suddenly gets worse, the chest pain gets worse, you cough up blood, you feel faint or you collapse, call 999 straight away. Don’t wait for a lift.
Worse breathing, worse pain, blood, fainting — 999.
Exactly. Can you tell me what you’re doing next?
Find someone to take me to the hospital this afternoon, ring you back if I can’t, and 999 if I get worse.
Perfect. I’m writing this call up now and sending a letter to the hospital team. I’ll ring you tomorrow to see how you got on. You did the right thing ringing.
SCA_MODELS.why: Documents, hands over and books follow-up

SCA_STEM.name: Ivy Marchetti
meds: COPD inhalers as on the repeat list
SCA_STEM.allergy: Not recorded in the booking note; check before any prescription
SCA_STEM.recent: Rang the practice: more breathless than usual. She believes it is another COPD flare-up.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call: “Could you call me in some steroids and antibiotics so I don’t have to come down?”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG115 (COPD in over 16s, 2018, updated 2019) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] NICE NG158 (venous thromboembolic diseases, 2020, updated August 2023) · [3] NICE NG114 (COPD exacerbation: antimicrobial prescribing, 2018) · [4] NICE NG106 (chronic heart failure, 2018, updated September 2025) · [5] NICE NG250 (pneumonia, September 2025; partly replaced CG191) · [7] GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: More breathlessness in known COPD is not automatically a flare. Ask the questions that separate an infective exacerbation from PE, heart failure, pneumonia and pneumothorax. Sudden onset, pleuritic pain and a swollen calf after a long journey is a PE picture: same-day hospital assessment, not a phoned-in prescription.

points.h: What a typical flare looks like
points.t: A COPD exacerbation is a sustained worsening beyond normal day-to-day variation, usually building over days, with more breathlessness, more cough and often more or discoloured sputum. NICE NG115 [1] lists factors favouring hospital care, including severe breathlessness, rapid onset, poor general condition, cyanosis, confusion or drowsiness, worsening oedema and poor social support.

Sudden onset, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, unilateral calf pain or swelling, and risk factors (immobility, long journeys, recent surgery, cancer, previous VTE). NICE NG158 [2] uses the two-level PE Wells score: more than 4 points means PE likely, needing an immediate CTPA, or interim therapeutic anticoagulation if the scan is delayed. Signs of DVT and PE as the most likely diagnosis score 3 each, so on this history she is very likely to be PE-likely. D-dimer is the test for the PE-unlikely group, not for her.

Heart failure: orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal breathlessness, ankle swelling, weight gain (NICE NG106 [4]). Pneumonia: fever, new focal or pleuritic pain, confusion; CRB65 guides severity in primary care (NICE NG250 [5]). Pneumothorax: sudden one-sided pain and breathlessness. Arrhythmia: palpitations, dizziness.

On the phone you can judge speech, confusion and the story, but not pulse, oxygen saturation, chest signs, calf signs or an ECG. Any red-flag feature, or doubt about severity, means she must be seen in person, and the setting depends on the working diagnosis.

Only for a gradual, typical flare with no red flags and a patient who is coping. NICE NG115 [1]: prednisolone 30 mg once daily for 5 days when breathlessness interferes with daily activities. NICE NG114 [3]: an antibiotic is a judgement based on sputum colour change and increased volume or thickness, severity and risk; not every flare needs one. Remote prescribing should follow GMC guidance [7] on adequate assessment.

NICE NG12 [6]: people aged 40 and over with unexplained haemoptysis are referred on a suspected cancer pathway; chest X-ray thresholds are lower for people who have ever smoked. Ask about haemoptysis and weight loss in every breathless COPD call.

Suspected PE with a stable patient: same-day hospital assessment arranged by the GP (e.g. acute medical take or same-day emergency care, by local pathway). Unstable, very breathless, collapsing or chest pain getting worse: 999. Tell her not to drive herself.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start; acknowledged her request and exhaustion before asking permission for focused questions.
Mobility since the coach trip, who is with her, transport, and how exhausted she is.
Picked up “not like my usual”, the sore calf she had put down to a knock, and “too wiped out to come”.
Idea (usual flare), concern (hassle, exhaustion), expectation (phoned-in steroids and antibiotics).
Recognised that pulse, saturations, chest and calf examination, ECG, bloods and CTPA are needed and cannot be done by phone.
Infective flare versus PE, heart failure, pneumonia, pneumothorax, arrhythmia and lung cancer.
Asked onset, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, calf swelling, VTE risk factors, fever, orthopnoea, confusion and palpitations.
Named a likely PE (PE-likely on NG158 Wells from the history) rather than a COPD flare.
Same-day hospital assessment arranged by the GP, transport solved, no steroid or antibiotic prescription.
Did not let the COPD label hide a new problem; would reserve remote flare treatment for a typical flare with no red flags.
999 triggers named, teach-back, call documented, hospital informed and a call-back booked.

social.t: Tiredness, minimising and practical problems with getting there drive the request to be treated by phone. Solving the practical barrier often ends the disagreement.
Ask who is with her and who can take her. Poor social support is one of the NICE NG115 factors that favour hospital care.

legal.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe remotely only when you have enough information to be satisfied the medicine is safe and needed. Here you do not.
If she refused to go, assess her capacity for that decision (Mental Capacity Act 2005), explain the risks clearly, give 999 advice and document. A capacitous refusal is hers to make.

professional.t: Record the questions asked, positive and negative answers, the working diagnosis, the disposition and the safety-net given. Handover to the receiving team should include the PE concern.
Diagnostic momentum and anchoring on a known long-term condition are recognised causes of missed PE. Asking “what else could this be?” is part of good clinical care (GMC Good medical practice, 2024).

community.t: Patient transport rules vary locally; family, neighbours or a taxi may be quicker. For COPD support after the acute episode: Asthma + Lung UK and local pulmonary rehabilitation.

redFlags: Sudden onset, pleuritic chest pain, unilateral calf swelling, recent long journey or immobility (PE)
Haemoptysis or weight loss (PE; lung cancer — NICE NG12)
Fever, focal pain, confusion (pneumonia); orthopnoea and oedema (heart failure); sudden one-sided pain (pneumothorax)
Unable to speak in sentences, collapse, confusion or drowsiness — 999
psychosocial: Exhaustion and not wanting the fuss
Who is at home and how she will get to hospital
ice: Concern: the hassle of going in when she is exhausted
Expectation: steroids and antibiotics called in by phone

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This doesn’t sound like your usual flare. Sudden breathlessness with a sharp pain on breathing and a swollen calf after a long journey makes me worried about a blood clot in the lung, and that needs checking today.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “A clot can form in a leg vein when you’ve been sitting still for a long time, and a piece can travel to the lung. It causes sudden breathlessness and a sharp pain on breathing. It needs a scan to find it, and it’s treated with blood thinners, not steroids.”

management.reflectIce: “I know you hoped I could sort this by phone, and I know you’re exhausted. That’s exactly why I want to make getting there as easy as possible.”
management.psychosocial: Take on the practical barrier: transport, someone to go with her, the hospital expecting her. Do not let tiredness or minimisation change the disposition.
sharedPlan: Same-day hospital assessment for suspected PE (NICE NG158: PE-likely on Wells → CTPA or interim anticoagulation)
No steroid or antibiotic prescription today; the hospital manages treatment
Call documented; hospital team informed; GP call-back tomorrow
safetyNet: 999: sudden worse breathlessness, worse chest pain, coughing blood, fainting or collapse
Ring back straight away if she cannot get a lift

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This telephone station is failed by accepting the patient’s diagnosis. The marks are in the discriminating questions, a safe disposition, and getting a tired, reluctant patient to hospital.

items.fail: Issuing prednisolone and an antibiotic because she has COPD and says it is a flare.
items.why: “Fails to consider serious alternative diagnoses.” A new cause of breathlessness in COPD is easily hidden by the label.
items.fix: Ask onset first: “Gradual over days, or suddenly?” Then pleuritic pain, calf, travel.

items.fail: Finding the PE features but arranging a D-dimer at the surgery tomorrow.
items.why: NICE NG158: with PE likely (Wells more than 4), the next step is an immediate CTPA or interim anticoagulation, not a D-dimer.
items.fix: Same-day hospital assessment, arranged by you, today.

items.fail: Forgetting to ask about heart failure, pneumonia and haemoptysis once PE is suspected.
items.why: A focused screen of the other mimics shows structured reasoning and informs the handover.
items.fix: One grouped question: fever, ankle swelling, sitting up at night, racing heart, blood in the phlegm.

items.fail: Arguing: “You must go to hospital” repeated louder when she objects.
items.why: “Does not explore or respond to the patient’s concerns.” Her objection is practical and emotional.
items.fix: “What would make it easier to go?” Then take on the transport.

items.fail: Colluding: agreeing to “see how she goes overnight” because she is exhausted.
items.why: Unsafe disposition outweighs any rapport gained.
items.fix: Be honest and warm: “I wouldn’t ask if I didn’t think it mattered today.”

items.fail: Ending with “call back if worse” and no documentation or handover.
items.why: Telephone consultations are marked on explicit safety-netting and continuity.
items.fix: Name the 999 triggers, check teach-back, tell her the hospital is expecting her, book a call-back.
